9 October 2026 — A properness certificate with coprime leading monomials belongs to a satisfiable system

Working proofs of two structural facts about certificates; the review's test ends with neither a certificate nor a kill. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the review asked, on the LCM-lattice lead: for one structured unsatisfiable system exhibit a set \(G\) with mostly coprime leading monomials satisfying the pair condition of the truncated Buchberger criterion up to a stated cutoff, or prove that every such \(G\) forces a cutoff a constant fraction below half. Before choosing a system: how coprime can the leading monomials of a certificate for an unsatisfiable system be at all?

Architecture test. Outcome of the decisive test named in the method-gap review: neither branch. No certificate for a structured system is exhibited. The kill condition as stated is false without a width restriction, since axioms of degree above the cutoff give a trivial certificate at any cutoff, and for bounded-degree axioms no bound on the cutoff is obtained. What is obtained limits the form of any certificate: coprime leading monomials together with resolved Boolean pairs are impossible for unsatisfiable systems, and a certificate with elements of degree at most \(D\) must contain an element of degree \(D\) or two overlapping elements of total degree at least \(D+2\).

New mathematics. If the non-Boolean elements of \(G\) have pairwise coprime leading monomials and their pairs with the Boolean axioms are resolved, \(G\) is a Gröbner basis outright and, having no constant, its ideal has a Boolean zero. Hence a properness certificate at cutoff \(D\) for an unsatisfiable system with axioms and generators of degree at most \(D\) contains an unresolved pair above the cutoff: either a generator of degree exactly \(D\) with a Boolean axiom, or two generators with overlapping leading monomials whose lcm has degree above \(D\), one of them of degree at least \(D/2+1\). Also recorded: a certificate, in the general sense of the truncated entry, exists whenever the closure is proper.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The facts constrain what a lower-bound proof in this format looks like; they give no family, no bound on the cutoff and no certificate.

General statement. prop:coprime-certificate-satisfiable holds over \(\mathbb F_2\) for every set of multilinear polynomials and every degree-compatible order; cor:certificate-forced-overlap for every unsatisfiable Boolean system with axioms of degree at most the cutoff.

Statements and proofs

Work in \(\mathbb F_2[x_1,\ldots,x_v]\) with a degree-compatible order. Let \(B\) be the Boolean axioms \(x_a^2+x_a\) and \(H\) a set of nonzero multilinear polynomials; \(G=B\cup H\). Pairs are resolved in the sense of the truncated Buchberger entry.

Proposition (coprime certificate satisfiable). Suppose the leading monomials of the elements of \(H\) are pairwise coprime, \(H\) contains no constant, and for every \(h\in H\) and every variable \(x_a\) dividing \(\mathrm{LM}(h)\) the pair \((h,x_a^2+x_a)\) is resolved. Then \(G\) is a Gröbner basis of the ideal it generates, that ideal is proper, and the polynomials of \(H\) have a common zero in \(\{0,1\}^v\).

Proof. Every pair of \(G\) is resolved: two elements of \(H\), an element of \(H\) with a Boolean axiom in a variable not dividing its leading monomial, and two Boolean axioms all have coprime leading monomials, and a pair with coprime leading monomials is resolved by the product criterion; the remaining pairs are resolved by hypothesis. Buchberger's criterion, or the truncated lemma applied at every cutoff, shows that every element of the ideal has a leading monomial divisible by one of \(G\). No element of \(G\) is constant, so \(1\) is not in the ideal. The quotient is then a nonzero algebra spanned by multilinear monomials in which every element is idempotent, hence a nonzero finite product of copies of \(\mathbb F_2\), and a projection to a factor is a common zero in \(\{0,1\}^v\). \(\square\)

Corollary (certificate forced overlap). Let \(\Gamma\) be an unsatisfiable Boolean system over \(\mathbb F_2\) whose axioms have degree at most \(D\), and let \(G=B\cup H\) be a properness certificate at cutoff \(D\): \(H\) multilinear without constant and of degree at most \(D\), every pair with lcm of degree at most \(D\) resolved, and \(\Gamma\subseteq S_D(G)\). The degree bound is no restriction: discarding elements of higher degree changes neither \(S_D(G)\) nor the pair condition. Then some pair of \(G\) is not resolved, and every unresolved pair has lcm of degree above \(D\). Such a pair is either \((h,x_a^2+x_a)\) with \(x_a\mid\mathrm{LM}(h)\) and \(\deg h=D\), or \((h,h')\) with overlapping leading monomials and \(\deg h+\deg h'\ge D+2\), so that one of them has degree at least \(D/2+1\).

Proof. If every pair were resolved, \(G\) would be a Gröbner basis without a constant by the argument above, which needs only that all pairs are resolved, and its ideal, which contains \(\Gamma\), would be proper, against unsatisfiability. Unresolved pairs have lcm of degree above \(D\) by the definition of a certificate. A pair of an element of \(H\) with a Boolean axiom in a variable of its leading monomial has lcm of degree \(\deg h+1\). A pair of two elements of \(H\) with coprime leading monomials is resolved; with overlapping ones, \(\deg\operatorname{lcm}\le\deg h+\deg h'-1\). \(\square\)

Existence of certificates. In the general sense of the truncated entry, a set \(G\) with the pair condition, without the form \(B\cup H\): if \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\), then \(G=C_D(\Gamma)\setminus\{0\}\) is one. For \(g,h\) in it with lcm \(L\) of degree at most \(D\), the S-polynomial is a combination of monomial multiples of \(g\) and \(h\) of degree at most \(\deg L\le D\), so it lies in \(C_D(\Gamma)\); if it is zero the empty sum represents it, and otherwise it is its own standard representation, its leading monomial being below \(L\). Conversely, by the lemma, a set \(G\) with the pair condition, without a constant and with the elements of \(\Gamma\) of degree at most \(D\) in \(S_D(G)\) gives \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\), since \(S_D(G)\) is then closed and contains the closure; \(G\subseteq C_D(\Gamma)\) is not needed for this direction. So \(1\notin C_D(\Gamma)\) if and only if such a set exists. A certificate of the form \(B\cup H\) with \(H\) multilinear is obtained, for \(D\ge2\), from the multilinear elements of the closure; this variant is not written out. The point was made by the reviewer of the preceding review: the format loses nothing, and the content of any lower bound is the description of the leading monomials.

What it says about the search

For axioms of bounded degree \(w\), a certificate at cutoff \(D\gg w\) of the form in the corollary must contain at least one element of degree above \(D/2\) that is not an axiom, overlapping another, or an element of degree exactly \(D\). The axioms alone never suffice, and coprimality can describe only part of the set. The corollary forces one or two such elements, not a family; that a lower-bound proof for a structured system will have to describe many of them is my expectation and is not shown. Nothing here says how large the cutoff can be.

The kill condition of the review is not established and is false in the unrestricted form: if every non-Boolean axiom has degree above \(D\), then \(H=\emptyset\) is a certificate, as for wide rows. With axioms of degree at most \(w\) fixed, whether certificates can reach half of the free dimension is the open statement itself.

Specification decision. No change. The corollary is a property of certificates, not of formulas, and weakens nothing.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer confirmed the proposition and the core of the corollary, including every coprimality claim, the step to a common zero and the degree arithmetic, and required corrections that are applied: the certificate in the corollary has generators of degree at most \(D\), without loss; the existence statement is for the general certificate notion, covers a zero S-polynomial, and names the hypotheses each direction uses; "full coprimality is impossible" is restated; the product-tree sentence and the word "family" are removed or marked as expectation. Unused: multilinearity and the field \(\mathbb F_2\) in the proposition. Dependency reread: the truncated Buchberger entry. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. Second entry on this lead. Next attempt, concrete: take the smallest structured unsatisfiable family for which the derived elements of degree above \(D/2\) can be written in closed form, two contradictory parity-defined rows on disjoint blocks joined by one shared form, and write its certificate; this is a calculation, not a search.

9 October 2026 — Two contradictory rows are refuted by a sum of their axioms, whatever they share

Working proof that two-row systems have refutation degree at most their width; the calculation named for the lead is trivial. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the preceding entry named a calculation for the LCM-lattice lead: write the certificate or the refutation for two contradictory rows sharing one form, as a function of their immunity, and read off the cutoff. The hope was a smallest structured system whose certificate has elements of degree above half the cutoff in closed form. If the cutoff of every two-row system is bounded by the row width, the smallest interesting structure needs at least three rows arranged in a cycle.

New mathematics. For any two relations in canonical encoding that are jointly unsatisfiable, \(1\) is a linear combination of their axioms with constant coefficients. The refutation degree is at most the larger width, independently of immunity and of how many variables or forms the rows share. So no certificate above the width exists for two rows.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The result removes two-row systems of small width as test structures and says nothing about a family.

General statement. prop:two-row-axiom-identity holds over every field for every pair of jointly unsatisfiable relations on arbitrary variable sets.

The identity

For a set \(X\) of Boolean variables and \(\tau\in\{0,1\}^X\) let \(\chi_\tau=\prod_{i\in X}(x_i\text{ if }\tau_i=1,\ 1-x_i\text{ if }\tau_i=0)\), the indicator of \(\tau\), of degree \(|X|\). A row is a relation \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\); its canonical axioms are the \(\chi_\tau\) for \(\tau\notin R\).

Proposition (two row axiom identity). Let \(R_A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_A}\) and \(R_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_B}\) have no common extension to \(X_A\cup X_B\). Then there are sets \(N_A\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_A}\setminus R_A\) and \(N_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X_B}\setminus R_B\) with

\[\sum_{\tau\in N_A}\chi_\tau+\sum_{\tau'\in N_B}\chi_{\tau'}=1\]

as polynomials. In particular the system has a Nullstellensatz refutation of degree at most \(\max\{|X_A|,|X_B|\}\) with constant multipliers, without use of the Boolean axioms, and \(1\in C_D\) for that \(D\).

Proof. Put \(T=X_A\cap X_B\) and let \(P_A,P_B\subseteq\{0,1\}^T\) be the projections of the two relations. They are disjoint: a common point extends to a tuple of \(R_A\) and to a tuple of \(R_B\), which agree on \(T\) and so glue. For any \(X\supseteq T\) and \(t\in\{0,1\}^T\), \(\sum_{\tau\in\{0,1\}^X,\ \tau|_T=t}\chi_\tau=\chi_t\), since \(\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}}(x_i\text{ or }1-x_i)=1\) for each variable outside \(T\). Let \(N_A\) be the tuples on \(X_A\) whose restriction to \(T\) lies in \(P_B\), and \(N_B\) the tuples on \(X_B\) whose restriction lies outside \(P_B\). A tuple of \(N_A\) is not in \(R_A\), as its restriction is not in \(P_A\); a tuple of \(N_B\) is not in \(R_B\). Then \(\sum_{N_A}\chi_\tau=\sum_{t\in P_B}\chi_t\) and \(\sum_{N_B}\chi_{\tau'}=\sum_{t\notin P_B}\chi_t\), and the two sums add to \(\sum_{t\in\{0,1\}^T}\chi_t=1\). If \(T=\emptyset\) the same reads with a one-point space, and one of the relations is empty. \(\square\)

For rows on linear forms over \(\mathbb F_2\), with coefficient field of characteristic two, the same holds with width counting forms when the distinct forms of both rows are linearly independent, after a linear change of coordinates, which preserves degree. That condition is sufficient and not necessary.

Consequence for certificates. For two jointly unsatisfiable rows no closure is proper at the larger width, so no properness certificate exists there. Immunity does not enter: the identity uses the axioms as given and no multiplication. More generally a system with a proper closure above its width has no two rows that are jointly contradictory. The identity does not extend to one row against the rest of a larger system: the projections onto the shared variables are disjoint there too, but the indicators on the rest's side are not axioms and may be costly to derive. Which three-row structures are the smallest not covered is not determined here.

Specification decision. No change; nothing is weakened. The proposition is not a new condition: under the specification's requirement that every variable lies in at least two blocks, a two-row system has both rows on all variables, and the bound is then the number of variables and says nothing.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer confirmed the proposition and its proof over any field and required corrections to the prose, all applied: "at most" in the degree; the linear-forms remark needs characteristic two and independence of the distinct forms; the sentence on tree-like overlaps and cycles was an overclaim and is replaced; the specification sentence did not make sense and is rewritten; the scope is two-row systems of small width. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. The lead asked for a costed lift of the lcm relations to organize the calculation of when a closure stays proper. It has given the truncated criterion, the equivalence of certificates with properness, the forced overlap, and this bound for its named test structure. Its queued sub-ideas are still open, so it is not developed: the next attempt is the first of them, the pair-condition checker, to be built against the three-row structure below so that a claimed certificate there can be verified exactly. This is the third entry of the lead's spell of four.

9 October 2026 — A truncated completion tool gives exact refutation degrees: three for parity 2-clauses up to sixteen variables

Finite check with a new tested tool; exact degrees at small sizes, the three-row structure not reached. Queue development of the LCM-lattice lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the last entry of the LCM-lattice lead's spell was to build the pair-condition checker of the truncated Buchberger criterion and use it on a three-row structure. The measured parity 2-clause instances had only upper bounds on their refutation degree. Does a completion that adds S-polynomial remainders within the cutoff give the exact degree in practice, and does it agree with the static values?

New mathematics. A finite check. The tool tools/truncated_buchberger.py completes a generating set under the pair condition within degree \(D\) and reports whether a constant appears; a produced constant lies in the closure, and without one the criterion gives non-membership, so this decides \(1\in C_D\) exactly. For \(3n\) products of two random affine forms it gives refutation degree exactly \(3\) at \(n=8,10,12,16\), three instances each: no refutation in degree \(2\), one in degree \(3\). At \(n=12\) and \(16\) this equals the static value, so the static test did not overestimate there. The run at \(n=20\) did not finish within its time limit.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The check certifies lower bounds of three on small instances, the first lower bounds measured on this route, and gives no information on the asymptotic law or on any family.

General statement. The tool's correctness rests on lem:truncated-buchberger-closure, which holds for every system and cutoff. ex:parity-two-clause-exact-degree records the instances; the hypothesis they bear on is conj:parity-clause-semiregular-degree, still untested beyond small sizes.

The tool

Polynomials over \(\mathbb F_2\) are sets of exponent tuples; the order is degree, then the exponent tuple; the Boolean axioms are ordinary generators. complete(G, D) keeps one polynomial per leading monomial, and for each pair with non-coprime leading monomials and lcm of degree at most \(D\) top-reduces the S-polynomial and adds a nonzero remainder. Axioms of degree above \(D\) are dropped, as the closure requires. Each input is first top-reduced against the earlier ones, so it equals its stored remainder plus multiples of degree at most its own and still lies in the span of the stored set. Every added element lies in the degree-\(D\) closure: the S-polynomial is a combination of monomial multiples of degree at most \(\deg\operatorname{lcm}\le D\) of elements of the closure, and each reduction step subtracts such a multiple of degree at most the current leading degree. When no pair remains, the pair condition holds, so by the lemma the closure is the span of the multiples and contains \(1\) only if a constant was produced. pc_degree returns the least cutoff with a constant. check_pairs lists unresolved pairs of a given set. Nine tests are in tools/tests/test_truncated_buchberger.py, among them a comparison with an independent linear-algebra computation of the closure on forty random three-variable systems at cutoffs one to three, covering both outcomes; the framework suite passes with them (557 tests, 7.7 s).

Limits: pure Python, top reduction only, no selection strategy; meant as checker and reference for a few hundred leading monomials. Coprime pairs are skipped by the product criterion.

Exact degrees

Prediction stated in the script before the first run, for \(n=8,10,12\): the exact degree equals the static value with multipliers \(|T|\le D-2\), which was \(3\) at \(n=12\); a smaller exact degree would have shown the static value too high. The size \(n=16\), static value \(3\), was added in a second run with the same expectation.

9 October 2026 — With every variable in two rows the expansion theorems give at most a quarter of the variables

Working proof of a ceiling on what two named theorems can give; a limit of a method, not of the degree. Queue development of the sparse affine sources lead while draining. Produced by Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5, reasoning effort low).

Question. On near-half-family and the Boolean PC family statement, the queue's head is the sparse affine sources lead of the invariant architecture review: the growing-modulus modular source exists with all its structural properties, and what it lacks is "minimal-core control and a uniform degree theorem". Core control was supplied by later entries; the degree theorem was not. The only general degree theorems for rows on variables read in this session are Alekhnovich–Razborov's Theorems 3.8 and 3.13. Can either give a bound near half for this source, or for any source meeting the specification's requirement that every variable lies in at least two rows?

New mathematics. A ceiling for the method, by averaging over sets of rows. If every variable lies in at least two rows, then for any expansion parameters \((r,s,c)\) the matrix satisfies, the bound \(rc/2\) of Theorem 3.13 is at most \(v/4+s/2\) and the bound \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\) of Theorem 3.8 is at most \(0.0335v+s/4\), with \(s\) the row width. So for rows on variables of width \(o(v)\) these theorems stop at a quarter and at about a thirtieth of the variables, whatever the rows are.

Goal progress. Unchanged. The proposition shows that the recorded degree theorems cannot be the uniform degree theorem the lead asks for. It bounds a method and says nothing about the true degree of any source.

General statement. prop:two-occurrence-expansion-ceiling holds for every 0/1 matrix with at least two ones in each column and every \((r,s,c)\) for which it is an expander in the sense of Alekhnovich–Razborov; it concerns rows on variables, not rows on linear forms.

Setting

As read in the source in the private-direction entry: \(A\) is an \(m\times v\) 0/1 matrix, row \(i\) carrying a constraint \(f_i\) on the variables \(X_i\) of its ones. The boundary \(\partial I\) of a set \(I\) of rows is the set of columns with exactly one \(1\) in the rows of \(I\). \(A\) is an \((r,s,c)\)-expander if every row has at most \(s\) ones and \(|\partial I|\ge c|I|\) for every \(I\) with \(|I|\le r\). Theorem 3.8: for \(\ell\)-immune \(f_i\) with \(s\le r(\ell/4-(s-c))\), every refutation has degree above \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\). Theorem 3.13: for constraints forbidding a single tuple, degree above \(rc/2\). An \(\ell\)-immune nonconstant \(f_i\) has \(\ell\le\deg f_i\le s\), since \(f_i\) implies itself.

Proposition (two occurrence expansion ceiling). Let \(A\) be an \((r,s,c)\)-expander with \(1\le r\le m\), in which every column has at least two ones. Then

\[\frac{rc}{2}\le\frac v4+\frac s2,\qquad r\Bigl(\frac{\ell}{4}-(s-c)\Bigr)\le0.0335\,v+\frac s4\quad\text{for every }\ell\le s.\]

Proof. Let \(I\) be a uniformly random set of exactly \(r\) rows. A column \(x\) with \(d\) ones lies in \(\partial I\) with probability \(P_d=d\,\frac rm\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}\frac{m-r-j+1}{m-j}\). If \(d-1>m-r\) a factor is zero and \(P_d=0\). Otherwise all factors are nonnegative and each is at most \(\beta=(m-r)/(m-1)\), because \((m-r-j+1)(m-1)\le(m-r)(m-j)\) is \((j-1)(m-1)\ge(j-1)(m-r)\). With \(\rho=r/m=1-\beta\frac{m-1}m\le1-\beta+\frac1m\), \(P_d\le d(1-\beta)\beta^{d-1}+\frac dm\). For \(d\ge2\), \(\max_{\beta\in[0,1]}d(1-\beta)\beta^{d-1}=(1-\tfrac1d)^{d-1}\le\tfrac12\). The matrix has at most \(ms\) ones, so \(\sum_xd_x/m\le s\) and \(\mathbb E|\partial I|\le v/2+s\); some \(I\) of size \(r\) has boundary at most that, and expansion gives \(rc\le v/2+s\). This is the first inequality.

For the second, \(\ell\le s\) gives \(r(\ell/4-(s-c))\le rc-\tfrac34rs\). The expected number of ones in the rows of \(I\) is \(\rho\sum_xd_x\), and it is at most \(rs\). Hence, with the same \(I\) in expectation, \(rc-\tfrac34rs\le\mathbb E|\partial I|-\tfrac34\rho\sum_xd_x\le\sum_x\bigl(P_{d_x}-\tfrac34\rho d_x\bigr)\); here \(rc\le|\partial I|\) holds for every \(I\) of size \(r\), so it holds for the expectation. For one column, \(P_d-\tfrac34\rho d\le d\rho(\beta^{d-1}-\tfrac34)\), which is positive only if \(u=\beta^{d-1}>\tfrac34\); then \(\rho\le1-\beta+\tfrac1m\) and \(1-\beta=1-u^{1/(d-1)}\le\ln(1/u)/(d-1)\), so with \(d/(d-1)\le2\) the term is at most \(2\ln(1/u)(u-\tfrac34)+\tfrac d{4m}\). The function \(2\ln(1/u)(u-\tfrac34)\) on \((\tfrac34,1]\) has maximum below \(0.0335\), attained near \(u=0.87\). Summing over columns, with \(\sum_xd_x/(4m)\le s/4\), gives the second inequality. \(\square\)

The constants are not optimized; at \(d=2\) the maximum of \(2\rho(\tfrac14-\rho)\) is \(1/32\), up to the \(1/m\) term. The term in \(s\) cannot be dropped: three rows on all variables with \(r=1\) have \(rc=v\), the trivial case of axioms as wide as the variable set. Not used: the immunity hypothesis beyond \(\ell\le s\), and the side condition of Theorem 3.8.

What it says for the lead

The growing-modulus source of the lead and the balanced paired source have rows on variables of logarithmic width with every variable in at least two rows. For them Theorem 3.8 gives at most about \(0.0335v\) under any expansion and immunity they may have; Theorem 3.13 does not apply directly to modular rows, and for a clause encoding with single-tuple rows it gives at most about a quarter. The same holds for every source of the specification whose rows are on variables with width \(o(v)\); rows on linear forms and auxiliary affine equations are admitted by the specification and are not covered. So the "uniform degree theorem" of the lead cannot be either of these theorems as stated. Whether the source satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.8 at all is not examined. The statements of the two theorems are as read in the private-direction entry; the reviewer had no excerpt of the source.

Where the ceiling comes from: for each \(r\) some set of \(r\) rows has at most \(v/2+s\) boundary variables once every variable occurs twice, so \(rc\) is capped near \(v/2\). The quarter comes from the factor \(\tfrac12\) in Theorem 3.13. A theorem charging boundary variables without that factor is not excluded by this argument.

Specification decision. No change. Considered: dropping the two-occurrence requirement so that expansion bounds could be larger. It is a normalization of the specification with its own degree-preserving proof, and without it private variables can be projected away; the ceiling is a property of the method, and the requirement stays.

Verification gate. One fresh-context medium reviewer checked the proof by hand, including the hypergeometric formula, the factor bound, both inequalities and the maximum \(0.03342\) near \(u=0.8706\), and found the proposition correct. Corrections applied: the case of a vanishing factor; the error term is now \(s\), from the count of ones, so no bound on occurrences is needed; "a thirtieth" was false as an upper bound since \(0.0335>1/30\); the scope excludes rows on linear forms; the last paragraph claimed more than the averaging shows. Not checked by the reviewer: the statements of Theorems 3.8 and 3.13, taken from this session's reading of the source. Record: review.txt.

Follow-up. Continuing. First entry on this lead. The uniform degree theorem it asks for is not available from the recorded theorems; next attempt, on its first queued sub-idea: for a small normalized modular core, use tools/truncated_buchberger.py to compute the exact degree and the leading monomials of the closure just below it, and compare with the filtered half the source is proved to keep.

Sub-ideas

  • Decide whether the paired source satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 3.8 with some immunity and expansion, which would give it a proved positive linear degree, at most about \(0.0335\) of its variables.

Process assessment. The budget entry had estimated these limits in a random model; the averaging argument here needs no model and no assumption on the rows, and could have been tried first. The lead is old and its question was half answered by entries that did not close it; this entry answers the other half negatively for the methods at hand.
